name: Petit Verdot

lines.s10: Petit Verdot is the dark seasoning of red Bordeaux, and alone it is inky, with blackberry, violet and a firm grip.
lines.s20: Petit Verdot is a late ripening Bordeaux grape, used a few per cent at a time to deepen the colour and firm the finish of a blend. Bottled alone, from somewhere warmer, it is inky and full, with blackberry, violet and plenty of tannin.
lines.s45: Petit Verdot means the little green one, because in Bordeaux it ripens so late that some years it never quite does. So the Médoc uses it as seasoning: a few per cent of the blend, for colour, perfume and grip. Tasted alone it is blackberry, black plum and violet, with a pinch of liquorice. It is inky and full, with firm tannin and bright acidity. Warmer places ripen it more surely, and Virginia, Spain and Australia bottle it alone, aged in oak. Pour it with braised short rib, lamb shank or a hard, aged cheese. Even in a blend, a little changes the whole wine.
lines.sale: Petit Verdot is for the guest who finds Cabernet too polite: inky, violet scented and gripping. I would decant it and pour it with the short rib, or with anything slow cooked and rich.

glass.lead: Blackberry, black plum and blueberry with violet and liquorice, inky and full, on firm tannin and bright acidity.

ladder.where: The Médoc and Graves, Virginia, Margaret River
Australia's Riverland, Castilla-La Mancha and Jumilla, California

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, tannin high and firm, alcohol medium plus to high, body full.

home.home: Bordeaux, above all the gravel of the Médoc, where it is among the last grapes picked and goes into the blend a few per cent at a time, beside Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, for colour, violet perfume and tannin. In a cool year it may not ripen, so a guest seldom meets it alone there.
home.abroad: Warmer, sunnier places ripen it more surely and bottle it alone: Virginia, California, Australia's Riverland and central Spain. There it is inky and full, with ripe blackberry and blueberry, violet and firm tannin, usually aged in oak.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: cool room temperature.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl.
service.decant: Consider it for a young wine made from the grape alone, after tasting a sample.
service.age: Firm when young; a well made wine of the grape alone softens over five to ten years.

with.why: richness that takes the tannin and the weight
slow cooked meat softens a firm, dark wine
blackberry and liquorice suit strong meat
salt and fat round off the grip

labels.means: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot with Cabernet Franc and often a little Petit Verdot, wherever it is made.
An American name for blends of the Bordeaux grapes, Petit Verdot among them; it rhymes with heritage.
The grape named on the front label, as Virginia, Australia and Spain bottle it: dark, full and firm.

guest.q: I have only seen Petit Verdot in small print on a Bordeaux label. What does it do?
guest.a: It is the seasoning. A few per cent deepens the colour, adds a scent of violet and firms the finish, much as a pinch of pepper lifts a dish.

guest.q: Why is this bottle all Petit Verdot?
guest.a: It comes from somewhere warmer than Bordeaux, where the grape ripens fully. On its own it is dark, full and firm, so it suits rich, slow cooked meat.

guest.q: Is it the same as Petite Sirah?
guest.a: No, only the names are alike. Petite Sirah is a different grape, at home in California. Petit Verdot is from Bordeaux, with a perfume of violet and a tight, fresh grip.

compare.tell: Cabernet Sauvignon shows cassis, cedar and a leafy edge; Petit Verdot is darker and more scented, with violet, blueberry and a harder, fresher grip.
Malbec shares the purple colour and the violet but is plusher and softer; Petit Verdot is firmer, with higher acidity and more tannin.
Syrah brings smoked meat and black olive; Petit Verdot shares its dark colour, violet and pepper but has no meaty note, and its tannin is firmer.

profile.st: Opaque purple to black · Body full · Acid medium plus · Tannin high, firm · Alcohol medium plus to high
profile.fruit: Blackberry, black plum, black cherry and blueberry; riper and jammier from warm sites
profile.other: Violet and lavender, liquorice and cracked black pepper, cocoa and coffee from oak, leather with age; inky colour and a firm, drying finish
profile.tell: Inky purple, violet perfume and blackberry on high tannin with bright acidity: darker and more scented than Cabernet Sauvignon, firmer than Malbec
profile.regions: Bordeaux's Médoc and Graves, in small shares of the blend; bottled alone in Virginia, California, Australia's Riverland and central Spain
profile.confuse: Cabernet Sauvignon has cassis, cedar and a leafy edge; Malbec is plusher and softer; Syrah adds smoked meat and black olive; Petite Sirah is another grape, of California

cards.front: Petit Verdot: what does its name mean, and why?
cards.back: The little green one. In Bordeaux it ripens so late that in a cool year the berries may stay green, one reason it is only a small share of the blend.

cards.front: What does a few per cent of Petit Verdot add to a Bordeaux blend?
cards.back: Deep colour, a scent of violet, a note of liquorice, and firm tannin with fresh acidity: seasoning for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

cards.front: Where is Petit Verdot bottled alone, and why there?
cards.back: Virginia, California, Australia's Riverland and central Spain: places warm and sunny enough to ripen a grape that Bordeaux often cannot.

questions.q: A blind red is opaque purple black. It shows blackberry, blueberry and violet with liquorice, and a firm, drying grip with bright acidity; there is no cassis, no cedar and no smoked meat. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Inky colour, violet and blackberry on high tannin with bright acidity point to Petit Verdot. Cabernet Sauvignon would show cassis and cedar, Syrah smoked meat, and Merlot is softer.

questions.q: A guest reads 3 per cent Petit Verdot on the back of a bottle of Margaux and asks why so little is used. What do you tell him?
opts: It ripens late and is strong, so a little is enough
It is too pale to be used in a larger share
It is a white grape, added only for its scent
It is added only to sweeten the wine
questions.exp: Petit Verdot ripens late in Bordeaux and is deeply coloured and tannic, so a few per cent seasons the blend. It is a black grape, dark and dry, and adds neither paleness nor sweetness.

questions.q: A guest wants a bottle made from Petit Verdot alone. Under which heading of the list are you likeliest to find one?
questions.exp: Virginia is warm enough to ripen Petit Verdot and bottles it alone. In Pauillac it is a small share of a Cabernet blend, and Saint-Émilion and Chinon are made from Merlot and Cabernet Franc.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: in the Médoc it is a seasoning a guest seldom meets alone, and the bottles of the grape alone from Virginia, California, Australia and Spain are its life abroad. The plan's own reason reads never meets alone; the entry says seldom, since a never is more than the sources read can prove.

A thin grape: the profile is written here. The Régionale row gives acidity as the middle of three; the profile says medium plus, on the Médoc wine council's word freshness and on the trade descriptions read, which give bright acidity as one of the grape's marks.

The Codex's Virginia record lists Petit Verdot among grapes chosen for thick skins and loose bunches. Virginia's wine body confirms the thick skins and the late ripening; one grower's page read through search calls the bunches compact. The entry says nothing of the bunch.

The name, the little green one, stands on two trade references read through search and is the reading of Wine Grapes; the origin and the parentage are left out, since the sources read call both uncertain.
Washington was left out of the places that bottle it alone: the Codex's Washington record names it only in blends. Castilla-La Mancha and Jumilla stand on the Codex's Spanish records.
Lavender, mulberry and leather with age are tasting descriptions from the trade references, not from a regional body. No Creole dish is given: none of the seven suits a wine this dark and firm.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
